item.title: Meta Fined €805 Million in Italy Over Facebook’s Default Photo Gallery Access
item.description:
Italy fines Meta €805 million over Facebook’s access to Android users’ photo galleries without specific consent, affecting around 20 million people.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million. The reason is that the Facebook app for Android reached into photos, videos, and their metadata on Italian users’ phones without specific consent and without telling people properly what was happening.

“The Italian Data Protection Authority (Garante) has fined Meta Platforms Ireland Limited €805 million. Through the Facebook app for Android devices, the company accessed photos, videos, and related metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them.” reads the Garante’s announcement.

“The measure concerns the ‘Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook’ feature, available since 2023, which, while browsing, shows users photos and videos from their phone gallery as suggestions to post.”

The feature at the center of the case suggests photos and videos from users’ phone gallery as things to post while they scroll Facebook. It has been available since 2023. The Garante opened its investigation in July 2025, after a complaint from the Bolzano Consumer Protection Centre, and backed it with its own technical analysis.

The analysis found three main problems. Facebook used a single permission to access the phone’s photo gallery for several different purposes. The notice shown to users was unclear and did not explain that granting permission would also enable photo suggestions. On top of that, the feature was enabled by default.

This is important because, once users grant full access, the app can continuously read all the photos and videos stored on their devices. Neither users nor the Garante can see exactly which data the app accesses or uses.

“The checks revealed that:

  • access to the gallery is requested through a single permission, valid for the entire app and for several functions serving different purposes;
  • the authorisation is preceded by a generic notice (“enable other features”) that does not allow users to understand that they are also authorising gallery suggestions;
  • furthermore, the feature was enabled by default.” continues the statement.

Meta told Reuters users must grant device-level permission to enable the feature and can revoke it at any time through their settings.

“This is a simple feature ​that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook. ​Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and ‌they ⁠can change that permission at any time in their settings,” the company spokesperson said in a statement

The Garante pointed to Article 122 of Italy’s Privacy Code, which carries the EU’s ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats the smartphone as part of a person’s private sphere, so any access to what’s on it needs free and informed consent.

Meta argued that the Irish authority should have handled the case. The Garante said no, since the ePrivacy rules don’t include the one-stop-shop mechanism. The case also doesn’t cover whether Meta used any content to train artificial intelligence, which the company denies. The Garante did keep the option open to look separately at a new feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud.

Meta now has 60 days to fix things. It has to ask for consent through a separate, specific request, and explain what the feature does, that it involves gallery access, and how to turn it off. It also has to keep the feature off by default, even for people who already said yes. If Meta misses the deadline, it can’t activate the feature for anyone without valid consent.

The company also owes the Garante two reports. One is due within 30 days, on what it has started doing, and another within 90 days, on the measures it has adopted.

Several factors led to the high fine. Around 20 million Android users in Italy were affected, and the violation is still ongoing for users who have not updated the app. Meta had also been fined by the Garante in 2019 and provided only limited cooperation during the investigation.

One factor worked in Meta’s favor: the company changed the feature after the complaint. However, the Garante said these changes came too late and only applied to users who updated the app.

The fine represents about 0.47% of Meta’s global revenue. It is unlikely to cause serious financial problems for the company, but it may help give users more control over their photo privacy.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Meta)

item.title: The Microsoft Outage Left 15 Hotel Guests Poisoned by Chlorine
item.description:
A Microsoft 365 outage stopped a hotel’s email chlorine alert in Germany, and 15 guests were poisoned.

A hotel in Germany had a maintenance safety system for its sauna area. If the chlorine level got too high, the system emailed the operators. When Microsoft’s cloud services failed, those emails couldn’t go out, the chlorine rose, and 15 guests were poisoned, according to Notebookcheck report.

“Over a dozen guests at a theme park hotel in Germany were injured by excessive chlorine levels.” states Notebookcheck. “According to local media reports, the incident was caused by a problem with the email-based system used to control chlorine dosing, which was affected by the Microsoft outage.”

German emergency services sent 40 first responders. Local media reported that four victims were taken to hospital, and one stayed for further observation. An alarm that depends on email works until the email doesn’t.

“Guests at the Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Brühl, were injured as a result. They complained of health problems after visiting the pool. The pool was temporarily closed but has since been reopened, as the fire department informed WDR on Saturday.” states WDR. “Due to complaints from hotel guests, emergency services and the fire department were called. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation; ultimately, the number of affected individuals rose to a total of 15.”

The incident shows the danger of relying on email for critical safety alerts. When the email service fails, the warning system fails too.

The trigger was a global Microsoft outage from 12 to 14 November that hit Outlook and other services. Some Japanese workers went back to fax machines to keep their businesses running. The outage wasn’t as big as the CrowdStrike failure in 2024, which disrupted a huge number of corporate computers, but this one hurt people. Tom’s Hardware notes it could have ended in something worse if the problem hadn’t been caught earlier.

This incident is a warning for anyone who relies on online services or connected devices to manage safety systems. An alarm that depends entirely on the internet can fail when the connection or cloud service goes down. In this case, the hotel had only one way to send warnings, and that system stopped working.

The solution is to have a physical or offline backup that continues to work even when internet services are unavailable. Staff must also know how to use it and practice regularly.

“This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety.” states Tom’ss Hardware. “Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline.”

A backup that nobody knows how to operate is useless. Another option is to run the servers and automation locally, rather than relying on cloud services. However, this requires more work to build and maintain, and it does not protect against local problems such as power outages.

The incident also shows how much business now depends on a few large companies. Microsoft, Google and AWS can offer reliable service at lower cost than smaller rivals or an in-house setup. When one of them goes down, millions of businesses feel it, and economic activity can stall.

For safety systems, the advice is short: architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Microsoft Outage)

item.title: SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA Target Telecom Networks to Spy on Subscribers
item.description:
Researchers uncover two threat groups, SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA, exploiting mobile networks to spy on users and intercept calls and text messages.

Telecom security firm Enea published research on two threat actors, dubbed SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA, working inside mobile networks. According to the experts, SilentAir has compromised operators since before 2025; however, a link between the two APT groups is possible and unconfirmed.

“Sophisticated threat actors are compromising Mobile Network Operators to steal information and launch attacks on other operators and their subscribers.” reads the report published by Enea. “Enea detected ongoing activity in 2026 by LIMINAL PANDA, a threat actor previously identified. We also uncovered SilentAir, a newly identified actor compromising operators since before 2025. Links between the two are possible but unconfirmed.”

Mobile networks need to communicate with each other to support roaming, calls, text messages and mobile data. They exchange this information through signalling protocols, much of it over a shared IP network called IPX. This system allows operators to work together, but attackers can also abuse the trust between them to access mobile networks.

Security problems involving SS7 were reported in 2014, followed by attacks exploiting the Diameter protocol. More recently, researchers have also identified attacks targeting GTP, another protocol used by mobile networks. This is particularly relevant because the GTPDoor malware uses it to communicate secretly with attackers.

GTPDoor is a Unix-based malware that uses the GTP-C protocol to receive hidden commands from attackers. HaxRob first analyzed it in February 2024. Palo Alto Networks later linked it to a threat cluster tracked as CL-STA-0969, which shares many characteristics with a group known as LIMINAL PANDA, tracked by CrowdStrike. In 2024, CrowdStrike assessed with low confidence that the group had links to China. Brandefence later reported with moderate confidence that some members may work for a regional office of China’s Ministry of State Security. In July 2026, POST Luxembourg reported the first detection of GTP-C attacks involving this malware.

Enea says its GTP firewall caught GTPDoor and related activity at several customers from the first quarter of 2026, and blocked it. It saw several hundred attempted covert sessions. It has directly seen or strongly suspects 5 to 10 infected operators, and believes there may be several dozen worldwide, mostly in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

The sessions carried commands to start and stop data tunnels, move sideways inside the operator, launch SSH, check the malware’s health and hide traces by deleting files and altering timestamps. Early in an infection the attackers tried to open tunnels often, and later the gaps grew. Half the tunnels lasted under 21 minutes, and a few ran over 24 hours. That doesn’t match the daily scheduled script CrowdStrike described.

LIMINAL PANDA has developed a new version of its malware, called GTPDoor v3. This version hides in GTP-U, the part of the protocol used to carry data. This makes it harder to detect because GTP-U traffic is more complex, carries much more data than GTP-C, and receives less security attention. The malware still uses the same XOR key, but now relies on libpcap to capture network traffic. This method is less visible to standard system tools such as netstat and lsof. Another important difference is that GTP-U is also used in 5G networks, while GTP-C is not.

SilentAir uses a different approach. Enea assesses with high confidence that the group is a state-level actor rather than a commercial surveillance provider. However, the researchers have only low confidence that it is linked to China. SilentAir launches SS7 and Diameter attacks from compromised network nodes inside mobile operators in at least six Asian countries. Its operations target subscribers in around a dozen other countries and territories. Taiwan is the main target, including political figures and government officials.

The attack mix gives it away. Interception makes up 18.30% of SilentAir’s activity, against 2.07% for typical surveillance firms. Those firms favor information harvesting (61.89%) and location tracking (30.90%), while SilentAir does 7.21% and 0.22%. The attacks come in bursts, from a handful of subscribers up to several thousand in a month, then go quiet for months.

For interception, the attacker moves a target’s registered location to a node it controls, so later calls and texts pass through it. Enea saw two-factor codes arrive right after interception for some targets, which suggests the goal is to break into their other accounts. Unlike the Russian-linked HiddenArt, SilentAir really runs the compromised nodes and answers transactions it started. Enea couldn’t analyze the binary because the operators kept tight discipline.

Silent SMS, which shows no alert on the phone, is the odd part. Most go to Taiwanese subscribers around midnight, and they probably test whether interception is still working, since phones are least likely to re-register then. They’re sent through a middleman SMS center and carry cheerful spam like health wishes, in case a carrier strips the silent flag and the message appears. Nobody should be suspicious of a stranger wishing them a strong body and a calm mind, which is exactly the idea.

The China-nexus judgment rests on state-level behavior, the Taiwan focus, no targeting of Chinese networks, and activity that fits a UTC+8 workday. There are dips in the morning and evening, pauses around Chinese holidays and essentially nothing on weekends, and the targets include political VIPs. Enea rates this low confidence, so treat it as a lead, not a verdict.

Enea couldn’t confirm a link to LIMINAL PANDA. Timing sometimes overlaps in the same operators, and the targeting matches, and a trojan called SCTPE tied to LIMINAL PANDA sends SS7 and Diameter traffic. But SilentAir answers transactions SCTPE can’t handle, its operational security looks better, and its working hours differ slightly. Two China-nexus actors sharing access, or both having compromised the same operators, are equally possible.

Enea says it helped customers remove LIMINAL PANDA activity, contacted other affected operators and warned those infected by SilentAir about malicious activity in their networks. Both groups have been stopped for now. Enea warns that access to one of the world’s 800-plus mobile operators can provide a way into others through IPX. AI also makes it easier to create new malware.

Enea recommends using GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls that share information with SS7 and Diameter security tools. Operators should go beyond industry checklists and monitor internal network traffic, where tools such as SIGTRANslator and Cordscan can go unnoticed. They should also connect telecom security with regular IT security. Outsourcing core network services can make investigations more difficult.

“The IPX interface must be regarded as untrusted. The evolution of signalling security has been based on the gradual realisation that the interconnect between mobile operators cannot be regarded as a trusted link.” concludes the report. “SilentAir and in particular LIMINAL PANDA exploits any available interconnect protocol, not just SS7, Diameter, GTP, but also other protocols like DNS, ICMP etc.”

The attacks come in bursts, from a handful of subscribers up to several thousand in a month, then go quiet for months.

For interception, the attacker moves a target’s registered location to a node it controls, so later calls and texts pass through it. Enea saw two-factor codes arrive right after interception for some targets, which suggests the goal is to break into their other accounts. Unlike the Russian-linked HiddenArt, SilentAir really runs the compromised nodes and answers transactions it started. Enea couldn’t analyze the binary because the operators kept tight discipline.

Silent SMS, which shows no alert on the phone, is the odd part. Most go to Taiwanese subscribers around midnight, and they probably test whether interception is still working, since phones are least likely to re-register then. They’re sent through a middleman SMS center and carry cheerful spam like health wishes, in case a carrier strips the silent flag and the message appears. Nobody should be suspicious of a stranger wishing them a strong body and a calm mind, which is exactly the idea.

The China-nexus judgment rests on state-level behavior, the Taiwan focus, no targeting of Chinese networks, and activity that fits a UTC+8 workday. There are dips in the morning and evening, pauses around Chinese holidays and essentially nothing on weekends, and the targets include political VIPs. Enea rates this low confidence, so treat it as a lead, not a verdict.

Enea couldn’t confirm a link to LIMINAL PANDA. Timing sometimes overlaps in the same operators, and the targeting matches, and a trojan called SCTPE tied to LIMINAL PANDA sends SS7 and Diameter traffic. But SilentAir answers transactions SCTPE can’t handle, its operational security looks better, and its working hours differ slightly. Two China-nexus actors sharing access, or both having compromised the same operators, are equally possible.

Enea says it helped customers remove LIMINAL PANDA activity, contacted other affected operators and warned those infected by SilentAir about malicious activity in their networks. AI also makes it easier to create new malware.

Enea recommends using GTP-C and GTP-U firewalls that share information with SS7 and Diameter security tools. Operators should go beyond industry checklists and monitor internal network traffic, where tools such as SIGTRANslator and Cordscan can go unnoticed. They should also connect telecom security with regular IT security. Outsourcing core network services can make investigations more difficult.

“The IPX interface must be regarded as untrusted. The evolution of signalling security has been based on the gradual realisation that the interconnect between mobile operators cannot be regarded as a trusted link.” concludes the report. “SilentAir and in particular LIMINAL PANDA exploits any available interconnect protocol, not just SS7, Diameter, GTP, but also other protocols like DNS, ICMP etc.”

item.title: German Military Grounds Quantum Systems Drones Following Reported Cyberattack
item.description:
German drone maker Quantum Systems confirms a cyberattack that disrupted operations, with reports pointing to a malicious software update.

Quantum Systems, a German defense company that builds reconnaissance and interceptor drones and the software that controls them, confirmed an incident in late October.

The company says its security teams quickly contained the threat while working with government authorities. It also points out that the incident does not pose a risk to customers or operators using its drones.

The company reported the incident to the relevant authorities, and an investigation is still underway with the help of internal and external cybersecurity experts.

“Quantum Systems identified a cybersecurity incident at the end of October 2026. An immediate internal investigation revealed an active cyberattack by hostile actors. The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities.” reads the company’s statement on cyber incident. “Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems’ unmanned systems for the end users and the operators.”

The manufacturer did not disclose details technical details about the security incident.

Quantum Systems added that European defense companies have faced ongoing cyberattacks for years, particularly those supporting Ukraine. It believes this support makes them attractive targets and says it has security measures in place to protect its systems and data.

“The European defence industry has been facing persistent cyberattacks for years. Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers’ security.” concludes the statement. “Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation plans in place and strives to fulfill the highest standard of data and system security.”

According to Der Spiegel and the Financial Times, citing internal sources, attackers may have used a malicious update file for QBase, Quantum Systems’ software for controlling drones and planning missions. This suggests that the attackers may have compromised the company’s update server in a supply chain attack. The incident is particularly significant because compromising the software distribution mechanism of a drone manufacturer can potentially affect the systems used by military and other customers, even without directly compromising the drones themselves.

Der Spiegel also reports that QBase is used to plan missions for the Vector reconnaissance drone, known as Falke in the German military.

QBase is Quantum Systems’ ground-control and mission-planning software for its unmanned aerial vehicles (drones). It runs on Windows computers and is used by drone operators to plan, execute, monitor and analyze missions. QBase is not simply an application for viewing drone footage. It is part of the operational infrastructure used to prepare and manage drone missions.

An unexpected software update reached customers and raised alarms inside the company. It is not clear how many customers installed it. Reports also say that the German military grounded Quantum Systems drones as a precaution and excluded them from a recent exercise. Military counterintelligence (MAD), Germany’s domestic intelligence service (BfV), and the federal cybersecurity agency (BSI) are reportedly investigating the incident.

However, these details have not been officially confirmed, and no attacker has been identified.

The incident highlights a major security risk for companies supplying software to defense and industrial customers: attackers can target not only the products themselves but also the systems used to distribute software updates. If hackers compromise an update server, they may be able to deliver malicious files to customers who trust the vendor and install its updates.

For this reason, companies must protect their software distribution infrastructure as carefully as their production systems. They should digitally sign updates, verify their integrity before installation, restrict access to update servers and monitor any unusual activity. Customers should also be able to independently verify updates before deploying them.

Another important measure is to have a way to quickly stop or roll back an update if suspicious activity is detected. In critical environments, such as military operations and industrial control systems, a compromised update can have consequences that go far beyond data theft, potentially disrupting equipment, operations and essential services.

item.title: ARTEX: How Cybercriminals Use AI Agents to Scale Their Attacks
item.description:
Amazon spotted AI agents running on ARTEX steal AI credentials and test deepfake ID bypasses.

Amazon’s threat intelligence team published findings on criminals running offensive campaigns with ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. Between 3 October and 5 November, Amazon’s MadPot network of decoy sensors caught requests from ARTEX agents. Some sensors posed as popular large language model APIs, and the agents sent them their own campaign records.

“The ARTEX agents sent these requests to MadPot sensors configured to present as popular large language model (LLM) inference APIs, and the requests carried the agents’ own records of their campaigns.” reads the report. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed threat activity referencing potentially affected AWS customers and notified them as appropriate.”

These records reveal what the attackers were doing. AI agent frameworks save previous conversations, so a single request often contained details of the entire operation, including instructions, tool activity, shared information and results reported by the agents. Amazon did not observe the attacks in real time and could not confirm whether the agents had actually achieved their goals. However, the records showed what the attackers were trying to do.

Amazon believes with moderate confidence that the attackers used ARTEX, based on references to the framework in their prompts and other technical evidence. It also believes with moderate confidence that several separate groups with links to China were involved. The evidence includes prompts written in Simplified Chinese, time-zone settings linked to China, targets matching Chinese interests and tools commonly used by China-linked groups. Some instructions told the agents to avoid targets in mainland China and government domains, and to route all outgoing traffic through proxy servers.

Operators set the mission and left the rest to the agents. Planner, worker, verification and compression agents shared a persistent knowledge graph, so each picked up where the others stopped. In one campaign, operators told agents to work through a fixed list of countries, favor enterprise production sites over personal projects and grade every credential. Keys exposed publicly for more than 30 days counted as low-value inventory.

The biggest campaign stole credentials for AI models, and it paid for itself. Stolen keys went into the framework’s own model gateway and powered the agents hunting for more keys. Agents also validated cloud identities, listed storage, checked permissions and went after managed AI services, secrets stores and application identities, with premium frontier models first.

The agents focused on applications that store API keys from multiple providers. A single poorly protected admin page could expose credentials for many accounts. The targets included API gateways and proxies such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API and LiteLLM, as well as AI development platforms such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama.

The framework included a set of instructions for attacking each product. These covered common weaknesses, such as installations that had not been properly configured, exposed admin pages, open provider settings and default passwords, including LiteLLM’s default master key. The agents also looked for known vulnerabilities, including CVE-2025-3248 in Langflow and CVE-2026-28797 in RAGFlow. Other techniques included bypassing authentication in One API-related systems by abusing the isCliRequest header, exploiting server-side request forgery (SSRF) to access cloud metadata services, and finding exposed secrets in JavaScript code, source maps, debug pages and environment files.

Discovery used internet scanners, certificate transparency logs and public code sources. Those included GitHub repositories and event archives, where secrets sat outside automated revocation, plus npm and PyPI packages, container layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites and Telegram channels. Credentials got a grade: L1 for a lead, L2 for a working API call, L3 for measured impact such as readable data or spendable balance.

The second campaign went after identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, using real-time deepfakes.

“In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to defeat the identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges with deepfakes.” continues the report. “The agents’ records show generating real-time deepfake video to pass live selfie checks and forged ID document photos to pass document checks.”

The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness check, which confirms a living person is present, and documented its face-detection events and coordinate system. Their best attempt put the face within 7 pixels of the target, and the vendor’s server still rejected the deepfake every time they recorded. Another session built a live deepfake pipeline on a single consumer GPU that reached 11.5 frames per second, close to what a live check expects.

They worked on ID photos too. The agents built fake camera metadata matching the real image dimensions and kept the original compression tables that re-saving would normally replace, so an edited image looked like an untouched camera photo at file level. At least four sessions ran at once, covering cash-out options, clearing balances, the deepfake pipeline and the bypass itself, and they swapped findings through shared tools. Nobody needed a coffee break.

Amazon informed the AWS customers it believed were affected by these campaigns. However, it could not confirm whether other organizations had been targeted. The company also published the IP addresses used in both campaigns, which were observed between 14 October and 2 November. Organizations can use these addresses to check their own systems for signs of activity.

Amazon advises companies to assume that attackers can quickly find exposed secrets and security weaknesses. AI applications, model gateways and inference endpoints should receive the same security protections as other production systems. Companies should also monitor unexpected costs and unusual usage.

The attacks took advantage of basic security weaknesses, including default passwords, exposed API keys, open interfaces and outdated software.

“None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker. The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software.” concludes the report. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.”

item.title: From Report to Tested Detection in Hours: The ARTEX Signature Pack
item.description:
The researcher MalwareMustDie released an open ARTEX detection pack in seven formats, built on behavior and a repeatable playbook, because attackers now turn weeks into hours.

The researcher MalwareMustDie released a public detection pack for ARTEX, the open-source AI pentest framework that criminals now run against real targets. He published it quickly because campaigns built on this framework are compressing intrusion timelines from weeks into hours.

The pack comes in seven formats: Sigma, including five behavioral correlation rules, Sentinel KQL, Suricata 7, Snort 3, osquery, YARA and a STIX 2.1 bundle. The IOCs expire after a year by design, and the behavioral rules don’t expire. If you read this as an IOC list, you’ve missed the point.

“The real release is the workflow: how to turn the next ARTEX-style attack into detections as fast as the attacker moves.” reads the report. “ARTEX is an LLM harness. Swap the model, prompts or infra and every IOC changes. What changes much less is how an agent behaves: machine-speed recon chains, ~1/s Password Sprays with rotating UAs, self-correcting API retries, systematic record enumeration. So the pack is behavior-first.”

ARTEX is a framework that connects AI models with tools. If attackers change the AI model, prompts or servers, the signs of an attack can also change. Many ARTEX indicators found on compromised systems are created by the AI model or the tools it uses, rather than being built directly into the framework.

For this reason, the researcher focused on sequences of suspicious actions rather than individual strings. These include automated reconnaissance at high speed, password attacks with about one attempt per second and changing user agents, API requests that automatically retry with corrections, and systematic searches through database records.

Every indicator in our detection plan goes through eight checks. These cover its source, reliability, classification, format and testing. Confirmed ARTEX indicators trigger alerts first. More generic indicators come with a warning and are never used alone to raise an alert. For example, the use of a curl user agent is common in legitimate traffic, so it should not trigger a security alert by itself.

Every indicator in the playbook passes eight gates, from source check to tier, format and testing. Confirmed ARTEX indicators alert first, and generic strings carry a warning and never fire alone. A curl user agent appears in plenty of harmless traffic, so nobody should get paged for it.

“Act on what the identity does, not where it comes from.” continues the report. “The Global Administrator grant came from Microsoft-internal private IPv6, so the ConnectWise app-ID rule now fires on role self-assignment or credential addition regardless of source IP. Source IP is enrichment only.”

MalwareMustDie tested the playbook on four campaigns, with an LLM helping and humans signing off every verification step. The ConnectWise Cloud Backup case from October 2026 shows why. A vendor’s app credential was compromised, and service principals then gave themselves directory roles, with one becoming Global Administrator from a Microsoft-internal private address. Microsoft said its own systems weren’t compromised, and attackers planted secrets that expire in 2028. A rule that trusts the source address would miss this.

The Korean financial case taught a different lesson. Attackers pulled about 25,000 records over roughly 30 hours, around 14 a minute, from peripheral systems like a broker loan inquiry service and an employee app. Volume thresholds miss that, so we count distinct records read per identity over time. The Japanese wave, reported by JPCERT/CC and GMO, exploited known bugs and misconfigurations, with no zero-days.

The expert also left things out on purpose. No backdoor trigger values, no private individuals and no victim names appear in the pack. Indicators he couldn’t verify wait in a hold queue until someone confirms them.

For network teams, the researcher added an experimental Zeek approach. One layer checks who you’re talking to, and another tracks what’s said and how often. Zeek can’t see sign-ins to Entra ID, though, because that traffic never crosses your perimeter.

The pack has moved since release. He updated it to v1.1.3 after traffic tests, added data from the FBI flash report that came out the same day, and confirmed Sophos X-Ops indicators that had been on hold. A chronology of public ARTEX reporting from October and November is in Appendix F. The quick Shodan scan on release day wasn’t comforting.

The full report includes the detection playbook, rules and indicators of compromise (IoCs). The expert encourages other researchers to test them, identify weaknesses and report both false positives and true positives.

Attackers use LLMs to complete in hours what once took weeks. Defenders must keep up with this speed while ensuring that humans remain involved in the process.

Defenders can use LLMs to compress “new report → tested detection” into hours too, as long as humans keep the verification gates.

item.title: Cognitive warfare: the new battlefield is the human mind
item.description:
Cognitive warfare uses AI, deepfakes and fear to manipulate opinions, erode trust and disrupt society.

Contemporary warfare is no longer fought solely through armies, weapons, and technological infrastructure. Alongside military operations and cyberattacks, a new dimension of conflict is emerging in which the primary target is people’s ability to interpret reality, distinguish reliable information from manipulated information, and make autonomous decisions. This is the context in which cognitive warfare takes root, a strategy that aims to influence the perceptions, beliefs, and behaviors of individuals and communities, transforming information into a tool of pressure and destabilization.

Unlike traditional propaganda, cognitive warfare leverages a much more complex technological ecosystem. Social networks, digital platforms, profiling systems, artificial intelligence, and psychological manipulation techniques allow for reaching different audiences with messages crafted to elicit specific reactions. The goal is not necessarily to impose a single narrative, but to influence the process by which people acquire information, form opinions, and evaluate events.

Multiplier of information operations and the manipulation of consensus

Generative artificial intelligence has further expanded the operational possibilities of these campaigns. The speed of content circulation, recommendation systems, and the ability to reach specific communities allow specific narratives to be amplified, even through coordinated behavior. It was not necessary to compromise the schools’ computer networks or damage infrastructure. Sending a single message was enough to activate emergency procedures, interrupt school activities, generate concern among families, and commit public resources. The human factor thus becomes the primary factor through which the threat’s impact materializes. School administrators, teachers, and law enforcement responded in accordance with their responsibilities, while parents and students were exposed to a situation of great uncertainty. In certain circumstances, it’s sufficient to exploit fear and human reactions to generate disorganization and social pressure. The new battlefield, therefore, isn’t just digital. item.title: Google GTIG Warns AI Agents Automate Exploits, Steal Credentials and Scale Cybercrime
item.description:
Google finds attackers using autonomous AI agents to automate exploits, steal AI access and scale intrusions, often sacrificing stealth for speed.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says attackers have moved past typing prompts into a chatbot. They now run autonomous, multi-agent frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI to carry out multi-stage intrusions faster.

“Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.” reads the GTIG report. “Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.”

The basic attack methods have not changed. What has changed is how quickly attackers can use them. These tools still rely on stolen credentials and systems that have not been patched. Amazon reached the same conclusion after monitoring its own decoy systems: None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. The difference is that AI agents can combine these techniques and carry out several steps without stopping.

These frameworks have three main capabilities. They can find and exploit simple vulnerabilities, ask an LLM to create custom payloads when needed, and change their approach based on the results they get. GTIG observed CAIRN and PentAGI being used in real attacks, while CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI were still being tested. CAIRN allows different AI agents to work together and share information through a common workspace. GTIG found evidence of its use against several targets, including organizations in the US aerospace sector.

CyberStrikeAI connects commercial and open-weight AI models to more than 100 security tools. HexStrike AI gives LLM-based clients access to over 150 tools, managed by more than 12 specialized agents. PentAGI is designed for less experienced operators. Between late August and early October, one attacker used a modified version of the framework to systematically scan organizations across Asia.

A China-nexus group also appears to be building its own framework. Others use ZeroHollow, an inference service for exploit development and routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework that runs code on its own. Google expects the trend to continue, since the barrier to entry is low and adding exploits is easy.

“We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations.” continues the report. “These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation.”

Vulnerability research is moving the same way. For the first time, GTIG saw attackers automate discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop. An exposed staging server hosted a framework called exploit_agent that compares popular web software before and after patches, drafts exploits and runs them. Victim data suggested interest in French media, entertainment and education sites, and the configuration notes were in Russian and told the operator to put the API keys in the file, not in the chat.

Once a vulnerability is patched, attackers have more information to work with. They can study the affected code, release notes, security research and proof-of-concept exploits to find ways to attack systems that have not yet been updated. Between January and August 2026, the number of vulnerability disclosures and exploits nearly doubled. Zero-day exploits also increased, from an average of 8 per month in 2025 to 11 in 2026, before reaching 22 in August.

The PaperCut case shows how quickly attackers can move. Two flaws were exploited as zero-days in late August, and Huntress and other researchers developed working exploits within 24 hours. GreyNoise detected an attack campaign just four days after the flaws were disclosed. In one case, attackers went from gaining access to obtaining domain administrator privileges within minutes.

The same pattern appeared with two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Researchers used LLMs to analyse the flaws, and details about the patched code and a proof-of-concept video appeared before the October 21 patch. Hundreds of exploit claims then emerged, but many did not work. Defenders had to spend time checking which reports were genuine.

LLMjacking is the money side. Attackers steal LLM credentials and cloud resources, then resell access. Mandiant handled incidents where fraudulent charges passed $100,000 in a day, and the worst reached $1 million before cleanup.

They got in with credentials from public GitHub repositories and fake sites that harvest session tokens. One actor used CVE-2026-40217, a LiteLLM sandbox escape that turns limited keys into admin credentials. Some created and deleted short-lived service accounts to dodge rate limits, and others started powerful GPU instances. In one case two attackers used the same credentials, and a botnet made millions of API calls in about 24 hours before they were revoked.

The loot goes to “LLM mixers,” storefronts that route buyers through pools of stolen credentials and compute.

“Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure.” continues the report. “This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”

GTIG saw prices from $0.10 to $25 per million tokens on Russian- and Chinese-language markets. APIMart multiplies prices by five above 100,000 tokens, and JetNight sells monthly subscriptions. Even criminals have a surcharge for long prompts.

Information operations now use LLMs as standard tools, and GTIG says so with high confidence. That covers state groups tied to Russia, China and Iran, commercial influence vendors and profit-driven networks pumping out political clickbait. Better content doesn’t automatically mean more impact, and profit networks can look like state campaigns.

In August, GTIG found a platform built on the Gemini API and other tools to automate personas, media, posting and distribution. Prompts asked for local slang and deliberate typos, grainy phone-style photos with no background text, and residential proxies with saved login cookies. Another vendor was building a platform for over 100,000 accounts using cloud phone farms and AI-simulated behavior to age new accounts, with plans to sell to its own government and foreign clients.

Nation-state actors use LLMs for productivity. The Iranian actor CALANQUE ION, formerly APT42, uses them for reconnaissance and social engineering, and Chinese actors use them for research, scanning and exploits. LEAKY CASTLE analyzes stolen data with them, others stage and exfiltrate through LLM platform file hosting, and North Korean IT workers use them for resumes and interviews.

MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE shows the creative end. Fake recruiter profiles with SynthID watermarks led targets to ClickFix lures, and the attackers then edited .claude/settings.json in internal repositories so that starting Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor. They also named access tokens after Microsoft Copilot. The Jieyou phishing service added an LLM chatbot in June so low-skilled affiliates can edit phishing panels in plain language.

AI tools also have limitations that attackers must consider. They can generate too much noise, make up details and even select the wrong targets. Groups focused on espionage are therefore likely to use them with caution, while cybercrime groups may accept a lower success rate in exchange for reaching more victims. Google SecOps has released detection rules for ARTEX, and Mandiant has published a guide to help organizations secure their systems. Our own analysis makes a similar point: Many ARTEX “indicators” found on compromised systems are generated by the LLM or by the tools it uses, rather than being built into the framework.

This makes attacker behavior more useful to defenders than looking for a single string or signature. When these frameworks run autonomously without tight controls, they leave traces in network traffic, recognizable identifiers and the code they execute. Google’s assessment offers some room for defenders to act: these frameworks currently trade stealth for velocity.
